item.title: Recent Outages Have Economic Causes
item.description: This essay originally appeared in The Guardian . It's an expanded version of the one I posted as " We Get the Infrastructure We Pay For ." It's been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We've seen outages at Microsoft , the FAA , a handful of banks , United Airlines , an unnamed classified NSA network , and Apple . People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyberattack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none. The incidents are unrelated. They're not the result of any cyberattack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don't seem to be the result of AI. (We can't say anything about the NSA; we'll probably never know the details of that one.) It's really just a series of unfortunate coincidences...

item.title: CISA Adds Three Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
item.description: CISA has added three new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-120705 OSGeo GeoServer XML Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-129243 OSGeo GeoServer Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability  CVE-2026-136716 Drupal Core Improper Check for Unusual or Exceptional Conditions Vulnerability  These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

item.title: ‘No reports, no strikes’: Russia’s pro-war bloggers slam proposed prison sentences for sharing photos and videos of Ukrainian attacks
item.description: Yesterday, a group of Russian senators introduced a bill in the State Duma that calls for prison terms of up to five years for illegally distributing information about the aftermath of Ukrainian strikes, as well as terrorist attacks and sabotage. Bans on publishing photos and videos of attack aftermath are already in effect in many regions, though until now the punishment has only involved administrative fines. Now a new article could appear in the Criminal Code as well. Authors of pro-war Z-channels and “military correspondents” reacted to the initiative with unanimous criticism. In their view, almost anything could be classified as illegal distribution, and the bill is aimed at eliminating “unnecessary questions” about how the state allowed this to happen. The Kremlin, however, said that “there is a war going on, and accordingly, the decisions that need to be made during wartime must be made to ensure security.” We present a short collection of Z-bloggers’ opinions on the new bill.

item.title: Vance and Rubio learn the price of loyalty to Trump
item.description: JD Vance and Marco Rubio are the Republicans most likely to run to succeed President Trump . But the past few weeks have shown how saddled each would be by decisions he made against their advice. Why it matters: Trump's unpopularity cost Republicans their congressional majorities. The Iran war and now the Jensen Huang imbroglio show how hard it'd be for Vance or Rubio to run on their own terms. The big picture: The problem isn't just that Vance and Rubio disagreed with Trump — it's that the two episodes cut to the core of their political identities. Vice President Vance has cast himself as a new-generation, anti-interventionist Republican who's wary of trying to solve the world's problems and has broken with GOP orthodoxy of unequivocal support for Israel. He made the case against going to war with Iran and blamed the war for the GOP's midterm shellacking. Secretary of State Rubio came up in the Senate as a foreign policy hawk and fierce critic of Russia and China, which sanctioned him in 2020. In May, aboard Air Force One en route to China, he warned Trump about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. What they're saying: In recent weeks, Vance and Rubio have had to confront the tradeoffs of serving under Trump in painfully public ways. Vance's post-election critique pinning the GOP's losses on the war reportedly frustrated Trump. Though the president agreed with Vance that voters chafed at high prices caused by the war, he pointedly noted his VP didn't say that going to war was the right decision. Asked last week, with Trump standing beside him, whether the war was worth the GOP's election losses, Vance declined to say. "I think the president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again. And my view is that my goal is and my job is to support the president of the United States," he said . When a reporter shouted a question to Rubio about Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia's president and CEO, the secretary of state turned around and walked away. Gerry Baker, Wall Street Journal editor at large, wrote this week in a column urging Rubio to leave the administration: "As it becomes evident that [Trump's] policy is shaming, corrupting and weakening America, [Rubio] has to keep fronting it while reassuring decent people he has nothing to do with it." The intrigue: Vance and Rubio were on opposite sides of the Iran war and the Nvidia debacle. On Iran, Vance opposed going to war but lost the argument. Rubio was and remains one of the most vocal defenders of the president's decision to attack — which could also be problematic if he runs in 2028 and the war is as unpopular as it is now. On Nvidia, Vance helped Trump engineer Huang's reinstatement despite reports that Rubio had warned Trump about the CEO. Yes, but: Neither man has said he's running for president in 2028, though Vance has long been expected to. He plans to wait until after the new year to decide, perhaps even until late spring. Rubio has indicated he won't run if Vance does. The two have become friends while serving together in the Senate and then the administration. The bottom line: Taking the jobs as the president's No. 2 and lead diplomat has had obvious political upsides for Vance and Rubio. The downsides are coming into focus as Trump enters his last two years as president.

item.title: America's new bargain hunt
item.description: Americans are getting choosier about how they spend their money, with new signs of a nationwide bargain hunt. Why it matters: Consumer spending has remained resilient, helping power eye-popping economic growth. But a closer look at spending patterns suggests that households are trading down, hunting for deals and second-guessing discretionary purchases. What they're saying: "Busy families are watching their budgets and being thoughtful about where they spend," Target CEO Michael Fiddelke said last week. Kohl's CFO Jill Timm said earlier this week that higher-income consumers are trading down to its stores, while middle-income shoppers are choosing its cheaper in-house brands. Customers bought more items per transaction but paid less per item, she said. Discount grocer Grocery Outlet saw signs for the first time last quarter of shoppers trading down from pricier products, particularly premium beef, CEO Jason Potter said. The big picture: Households this year have faced a fresh erosion of purchasing power after years of adjusting to a higher cost of living. That makes sustaining the same level of consumption increasingly dependent on finding cheaper alternatives. The hunt for cheaper alternatives may help explain why Americans are still spending at a healthy clip even as their frustration with prices deepens. By the numbers: Americans' spending is tilted toward cheaper retailers more than at any point since 2021, according to the latest Bank of America Institute analysis of its customers' card spending and deposit account data. It "suggests consumers are becoming more price sensitive," BofA economists wrote. "While households continue to spend, they are increasingly seeking discounts as concerns about higher prices persist." The bank says travel is the exception, with spending shifting toward pricier options. (Though it warns that may reflect some Americans forgoing trips altogether — leaving wealthier travelers to account for a greater share of spending.) Zoom in: Separate card spending data from Navy Federal Credit Union shows Americans across income groups are shifting toward discount grocers and warehouse stores and spending less at restaurants. Households are spending $167 more per month on housing, household bills and gasoline than they did in the same period a year ago — leaving less room in their budgets for other purchases. What to watch: Nearly three-quarters of holiday shoppers are holding off on purchases until Black Friday or Cyber Monday in hopes of better deals, according to Deloitte. A record share plan to shop during the promotional period, yet expected spending ($624 on average) is unchanged from last year. The bottom line: U.S. consumers' ability to keep spending may depend on how much further they can stretch each dollar.

item.title: As Corporate Bond Markets Grow, Is Bank Lending Shrinking?
item.description: The size of global corporate bond markets has increased dramatically over the past three decades. As of the end of 2024, nonfinancial corporate bonds issued by U.S. firms accounted for 29 percent of U.S. GDP. In other advanced economies, though bond markets remain smaller than in the U.S., corporate bonds were on average 11 percent of GDP in the same year. This growth is usually read as a shift from bank to market finance. But the ratio of bonds to GDP can rise either because firms take more debt in general, or because firms shift the composition of their debt toward bonds. In this post, we document growth in bonds to GDP for both the U.S. and other advanced economies, and argue that the sources of that growth are different across countries and have changed over time.

item.title: Built for trust and control: Powering the next wave of AI agents across Google Workspace and Google Cloud
item.description: For over 20 years, we have protected 4 billion users and 13 million organizations in Workspace, and critical enterprise and government systems on Google Cloud. From personal and financial records to board materials, regulated workloads, applications, and AI models, those safeguards protect what matters most. Blocking >99.9% of spam, phishing, and malware, alongside encryption and data residency, follows one principle: your data is yours, and you should always know and decide who can access it. That trust has powered one of the world’s largest developer ecosystems. Workspace APIs now handle more than 2.8 trillion calls a month, and public Google Drive API traffic alone is more than two-and-a-half times the volume of 2022. More than 18 billion reads from Drive each day come from API callers. Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed across email, documents, datasets, and cloud infrastructure, a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path. Today, Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI are generally available alongside Google Cloud Agent Gateway and unified protections across Workspace and Google Cloud. Builders get modern, agent-ready interfaces, and organizations get the visibility and control to adopt AI agents with confidence. Purpose-built interfaces: Workspace MCP servers, Workspace CLI, and Cloud Agent Gateway To help developers build reliable agents faster without forcing security teams to compromise, we are bringing agent-native interfaces to Workspace and Google Cloud: Workspace MCP servers : Now generally available, dedicated remote servers for Gmail, Google Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, and Tasks. Builders get one standard interface with built-in permission and DLP checks, and native human-in-the-loop (HITL) confirmations for sensitive actions. They also reject non-agent OAuth clients and work with Model Armor, Google Cloud’s prompt-injection screening service. Workspace CLI : Now generally available for local agents, terminal workflows, and automation, providing structured JSON outputs and scoped OAuth sign-in across Workspace services. Google Cloud Agent Gateway : A protocol-native gateway for LLM, MCP, and Agent2Agent (A2A) traffic on Google Cloud. It verifies Agent Identities against Agent Registry, enforces IAM policies and default-deny outbound rules, and screens requests with Model Armor. Together, these interfaces give AI agents open, protocol-native paths built on standards like MCP and A2A. Permissions, confirmations, prompt screening, and audit logging happen automatically, while traditional apps continue to run on existing REST APIs. Consistent controls across every agent workflow Those interfaces sit on a unified security model across Workspace and Google Cloud, with core controls shipping today: Policy checks on every request: Under our new Workspace AI Tools Addendum , AI agents must use Workspace MCP servers or the Workspace CLI rather than existing REST APIs. Technical enforcement begins on February 1, 2027, giving builders time to transition. Every call is checked against your organization’s Workspace permissions, DLP rules, and classification labels. On Google Cloud, Agent Gateway enforces IAM and default-deny outbound rules at the protocol layer and routes custom checks through Service Extensions to Identity-Aware Proxy, your own policy engine, or third-party security tools. Separate agent identities and limits: Admins and users need to tell an AI agent apart from a traditional app or a person, and cap what it can do. Agents connecting to Workspace must use dedicated OAuth client IDs , paired with least-privilege scopes, time-limited approvals (coming soon), and usage quotas (billing begins on April 1, 2027). On Google Cloud, agents receive their own Agent Identity in Agent Registry with no shared or long-lived keys, bounded by IAM policies and organization, folder, and project quotas. Those identities can also carry user-delegated authorization into Workspace when accessing mail or files. People stay in charge of high-impact actions: Routine work like creating drafts or summarizing documents runs autonomously, while critical changes require a person to sign off. In Workspace, MCP servers and the CLI enforce explicit user confirmation before agents send email, change Drive sharing permissions, or make bulk edits. On Google Cloud, policy can require multi-factor authentication or human approval before reading sensitive Cloud Storage buckets, changing IAM permissions, or modifying production infrastructure. Clear visibility and revocation: A one-time consent screen is not enough when agents run continuously. Workspace administrators can view, audit, and revoke AI agents in the admin console , and users will soon be able to view agent activity and revoke access to their emails and files. On Google Cloud, Security Command Center, Agent Observability, Cloud Audit Logs, and Wiz surface unusual behavior. Revoking a Cloud Agent Identity or OAuth grant stops access immediately. Boundaries for your most sensitive data: Coming soon in Workspace, AI access restrictions extend Workspace DLP and client-side encryption protections to agents. This will allow admins and users to block agents from accessing messages in Gmail and specific files and folders in Drive. On Google Cloud, VPC Service Controls, Principal Access Boundaries, and Context-Aware Access keep sensitive data inside designated perimeters and verified devices. Strict rules on your data afterward: Our new Workspace AI Tools Addendum sets clear boundaries for AI tools using Workspace APIs. It does not allow permanent raw storage, model training, extended retention of derived data, or API scraping. Derived and user data are removed within a defined window and when a user disconnects. On Google Cloud, Sensitive Data Protection masks sensitive fields before data leaves, and customer-managed or external encryption keys let you cut off access to Cloud agent memory stores immediately. Getting started Workspace developers: Start building with the Workspace MCP and CLI configuration guide , implement user confirmations via MCP and prompt-injection protection such as Model Armor, and review the Workspace AI Tools Addendum . Workspace administrators: Review connected apps and agents, configure DLP policies for your users, and monitor OAuth activity logs in the admin console . item.title: Enabling zero trust: ALLEN’s move to Chrome Enterprise Premium
item.description: Editor’s note: Founded in 1988 in Kota, Rajasthan, ALLEN is one of India’s leading coaching institutions, serving over 400,000 students across 350+ classroom campuses in 78 cities. Here, the IT and Cybersecurity Leadership Team shares how they standardized on Chrome Enterprise Premium to secure sensitive data and enable zero trust across over 5,000 users. With a workforce that lives in the browser across a SaaS and multi-cloud estate, securing our digital environment is paramount. Our 5,000+ users include faculty, operations, engineering, contractors, and a large Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) population. Operating at this scale, our top priority is protecting student personally identifiable information (PII) flowing through web applications. Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA), protecting this data is critical to regulatory compliance and maintaining brand trust. We needed security within the browser. The challenge of a fragmented browser estate We previously operated a mixed-browser environment, but managing multiple browsers made consistent policy enforcement and visibility challenging. We explored several options to standardize; however, our team didn’t want users to have to learn a new tool, and many of the options had high overhead costs. Testing and rolling out Chrome Enterprise Premium We implemented a phased Chrome Enterprise Premium pilot over a few weeks. Our team first validated the management capabilities in the Google Admin console by testing policy, deployment, extension controls, and reporting. Once we felt confident that Chrome Enterprise Premium provided our desired level of visibility, we rolled it out to several hundred users across various environments, including BYOD, Windows, and macOS. We deployed Safe Browsing and URL filtering for immediate threat protection, DLP rules to restrict copy/paste, downloads, and uploads on sensitive SaaS apps, and context-aware access to restrict application entry based on device posture. The proof of concept succeeded across all criteria including consistent policy enforcement, measurable reduction in risky-site and risky-download events, minimal user friction, and a centralized dashboard to give our teams visibility into managed user activity. The real decision moment came when we realized we could achieve a true Zero Trust posture. With Chrome Enterprise Premium as our backbone, access decisions now happen dynamically based on identity, device posture, and context. A teacher on a school-managed laptop enjoys seamless, full access. On a personal phone, that same educator can review materials without compromising security—downloads and clipboard sharing remain locked down. It delivers airtight data protection without disrupting daily instruction. A simpler, stronger foundation With Chrome Enterprise Premium, we replaced virtual desktops (VDIs) and fragmented security tools with built-in browser protection. Securing the browser itself means we no longer need to install heavy security software on every computer. This makes it easy to apply security policies to personal devices used by contractors and employees. Whether our team uses Windows, macOS, ChromeOS, iOS, or Android, we manage updates, policies, and audit reports from a single Google Admin console. Smart access controls Chrome Enterprise Premium ensures we only grant access when it is safe. Every time someone tries to log in, we verify three things: Identity: Is the user signed into their corporate account? Device: Is the laptop or phone managed and secure? Context: Where are they logging in from, and on what network? Stronger data protection We use Chrome Enterprise’s built-in features, such as Safe Browsing sandboxing and site isolation, and auto-updates to keep end users secure while they work on the web. These benefits plus Chrome Enterprise Premium prove that security does not have to slow down business. Employees work without security interruptions, and our IT team gets a single, clear audit trail across all devices. This helps us maintain high efficiency and supports our regulatory compliance efforts. item.title: High Stakes in Iraq’s Push to Reclaim Jurf al-Sakhar
item.description: High Stakes in Iraq’s Push to Reclaim Jurf al-Sakhar pfranz Fri, 11/20/2026 - 20:40 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Iraqi soldiers deploy in Jurf al-Sakher, in Babil Province, on November 20, 2026. AHMAD AL-RUBAYE / AFP Q&A / Middle East & North Africa 20 November 2026 8 minutes High Stakes in Iraq’s Push to Reclaim Jurf al-Sakhar On 20 November, Iraqi government forces entered Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of the Iran-backed group Kata’ib Hizbollah. In this Q&A, Crisis Group expert Lahib Higel explains the circumstances that allowed Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to restore state authority in this area. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Lahib Higel Deputy Program Director, MENA https://twitter.com/LahibHigel Related Tags Iraq What is happening in Jurf al-Sakhar? In mid-November, tensions escalated between Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s government and Kata’ib Hizbollah, an Iran-aligned armed faction, over control of Jurf al-Sakhar, a town on the Euphrates River in Babil governorate about 60km south west of Baghdad. The trigger was an intelligence report alleging that oil has been illegally extracted from pipelines passing through the area and transported to Baghdad for sale. The report suggested that this illicit activity has been taking place since 2021. Zaidi ordered an investigation, and a government committee entered the area on 13 November. It was led by the Hashd al-Shaabi, also known as the Popular Mobilisation Forces, an institution comprising volunteer armed groups that combined to fight ISIS in 2014. The committee also included representatives of the prime minister’s office as well as senior figures from various state bodies. The government subsequently announced that investigators had uncovered evidence of oil smuggling and unauthorised refining, prompting the prime minister to dismiss nine top security and oil sector officials for negligence. His government also publicly accused Kata’ib Hizbollah of involvement in the racket, allegations that the group rejects , claiming the investigation was politically motivated and aimed at compelling it to surrender its weapons. For the prime minister, the episode offered a prized opportunity to restore state control of Jurf al-Sakhar, which has been beyond the reach of successive governments since 2014. He ordered state forces to enter the area and set a 20 November deadline for Kata’ib Hizbollah to withdraw. The government sent reinforcements to Jurf al-Sakhar’s vicinity, and on 19 November the prime minister’s spokesperson issued a statement identifying the forces that were to occupy the area. These included Iraqi army units, federal police, energy police and two Hashd brigades.  Zaidi’s move proved successful. On 20 November, state forces entered Jurf al-Sakhar, following a deal in which Kata’ib Hizbollah agreed to partially withdraw its fighters and redeploy them elsewhere. That said, questions remain regarding the government’s ability to exert its authority over the area and the degree to which Kata’ib Hizbollah will retain influence there through the Hashd, of which it is a member. Why is Jurf al-Sakhar so important? Jurf al-Sakhar is a sub-district of Babil province, bordering Anbar and Baghdad provinces. It sits on an important route leading to Karbala, one of Iraq’s two Shiite shrine cities. The area became an ISIS stronghold in 2014, until state forces and armed groups that mobilised under the Hashd recaptured it in October of that year, displacing thousands of families.  The recapture of Jurf al-Sakhar had huge symbolic weight for Shiite forces, as it was one of the first areas from which they were able to expel ISIS. It also halted the jihadist group’s advance toward Karbala. The Hashd later renamed it Jurf al-Nasr (Victory Cliff), though not everyone enjoyed the fruits of victory: the battle for the area proved devastating to its predominantly Sunni population, which was forced to flee and barred from returning. Twelve years later, some 100,000 of the residents remain displaced . The duration and extent of mass displacement from Jurf al-Sakhar are unique among areas recaptured from ISIS, and the armed groups that took charge in 2014 have never previously turned it back to regular state forces. Jurf al-Sakhar was transformed into a sort of private militarised haven. In recent years, Kata’ib Hizbollah became the main authority there. The area provided the group with a strategic bastion where it maintained a large degree of autonomy. Prior to the fall of the Assad regime in neighbouring Syria, Kata’ib Hizbollah used Jurf al-Sakhar as a conduit for arms transfers from Iran to Syrian forces; the town is also where the group started manufacturing its own weapons, including drones. What drove the government’s confrontation with Kata’ib Hizbollah? The official justification was the investigation into alleged oil smuggling. But the clash stemmed in large part from Zaidi’s bid to strengthen the Iraqi state’s writ and bring armed factions’ independent command structures and weapons under government control. His move to take back the area has a domestic payoff, demonstrating to the Iraqi public that they have a prime minister willing to make highly controversial decisions. Foreign pressure also likely shaped Zaidi’s calculations. Washington has repeatedly urged Baghdad to curb the influence of Iran-aligned armed groups and their economic networks. Since taking office in May, Zaidi has sought to make progress on integrating autonomous armed groups and disarming those that refuse to come under state command. Following the withdrawal of U.S.-led coalition forces on 30 September, he outlined a nine-month disarmament plan. Most armed factions said they were willing to negotiate their status with the government and bring their weapons under central state authority. Two – Kata’ib Hizbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba – resisted. Relations between Zaidi and Kata’ib Hizbollah have been particularly fraught. Relations between Zaidi and Kata’ib Hizbollah have been particularly fraught. The group entered preliminary negotiations with the government, but rejected the prime minister’s plan in October. Tensions rose in early November when Zaidi cancelled service contracts at Mosul airport reportedly linked to armed groups, including Kata’ib Hizbollah, which in turn accused the prime minister and his family of corruption. According to media reports that cited leaked judicial documents, an arrest warrant was issued for the son of Kata’ib Hizbollah’s leader.  The oil smuggling allegations provided Zaidi with the legal justification to take action against the group’s de facto enclave. They also allowed him to attack Kata’ib Hizbollah at its weakest spot, namely the issue of public resources and corruption, rather than that of weapons – a more sensitive matter that the group would almost certainly have resisted from the outset. The prime minister’s overarching goal was not lost on the group’s leaders, but they calculated that it would be hard to challenge Zaidi’s anti-corruption campaign, which several political leaders endorsed at the start of his premiership.  Throughout the dispute with Kata’ib Hizbollah, Zaidi has sought judicial backing for his actions, aiming to portray the fight as a law enforcement matter rather than a political dispute. On 15 November, he met Supreme Judicial Council President Faiq Zaidan to discuss the oil smuggling investigation and possible legal measures against those implicated. Two days later, a judicial investigative committee entered Jurf al-Sakhar to look into any violations and inspect the sites identified in the intelligence report.  Zaidi’s gambit was not without risk, as Kata’ib Hizbollah could have dug in its heels, daring the prime minister to resort to force. Past episodes offer cautionary tales as to the outcome of such armed confrontations. In June 2020, government forces arrested fourteen Kata’ib Hizbollah members suspected of preparing rocket attacks, yet most were released within days following an armed mobilisation against the government. More recently, Zaidi’s own efforts to assert control of armed factions faced resistance, including an unsuccessful attempt to seize weapons from Harakat al-Nujaba in Baghdad in July. Moreover, Kata’ib Hizbollah was well aware that, in the past, Zaidi had made ambitious commitments from which he was forced to backtrack. He first pledged to disarm the groups by 30 September, only to extend the deadline to 30 June 2027 following pushback from hardline factions calling themselves the Islamic Resistance, including Kata’ib Hizbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba. How did Iraq’s Shiite political and armed factions respond? The confrontation exposed differences within the Shia Coordination Framework, the coalition supporting Zaidi’s government. All the Framework leaders were alarmed by the prospect of a battle between the state and the armed groups, fearing it could trigger intra-Shiite strife. Some appeared more open to taking the risk, believing that prior governments had been too cautious vis-à-vis the armed groups. Former Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki – who deployed troops to dismantle the Jaysh al-Mahdi armed group in 2008 – was one of those who seemed amenable to the use of force, at least as a last resort. Others, notably some linked to armed groups that had resisted the U.S. occupation, were more reluctant to threaten the use of force. One such person was Hadi al-Ameri, who heads both the military and political wings of the Badr Organisation. Differences aside, Framework leaders closed ranks in seeking to mediate between Zaidi and Kata’ib Hizbollah, with Ameri, Maliki and Humam Hamoudi, head of the Islamic Supreme Council of Iraq, all playing a part. The three endeavoured to convince Kata’ib Hizbollah to exit the area peacefully, advocating for the group’s gradual withdrawal in conjunction with the deployment of government-aligned forces, including Hashd units not affiliated with Kata’ib Hizbollah.  Kata’ib Hizbollah itself appeared somewhat divided. The group’s competing leadership networks – including those associated with its secretary-general, Abu Hussein al-Hamidawi, and those tied to Abdulaziz al-Mohammadawi, also known as Abu Fadak, who serves as the Hashd chief of staff – disagreed over the idea of withdrawal. Both rejected the government's allegations and maintained that the group needed to retain its weapons independently of the Hashd for the sake of Iraq’s defence. But, according to media reports, Abu Fadak favoured an agreement that would allow government forces alongside Hashd brigades to assume control of parts of Jurf al-Sakhar. In contrast, Hamidawi opposed any concession and allegedly proposed delaying a handover until June 2027, likely believing that Zaidi lacked the political backing to follow through on his threats and that other Shiite leaders would restrain him. Importantly, Iran stepped in to contain the confrontation. Zaidi made a brief, unannounced visit to Tehran on 6 November, during which he met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and parliamentary speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf. His meetings reportedly focused on Iraq’s efforts to mediate between Washington and Tehran, though it came amid growing U.S. pressure on Baghdad to rein in Iran-aligned armed groups. Ten days later, on 16 November, Esmail Qaani, commander of the Revolutionary Guards’ Qods Force, arrived in Iraq for discussions with Shiite politicians and armed factions, including representatives of Kata’ib Hizbollah. His efforts reportedly centred on avoiding a military confrontation between Kata’ib Hizbollah and the Iraqi government, partly by devising an off-ramp that would entail concessions by the group. What does the negotiated settlement look like, and are there risks of escalation? Withdrawal has been partially achieved without a flare-up of violence, which is no small achievement for Zaidi and the mediators. Broadly speaking, the deal entails legal action against those implicated in oil smuggling, Kata’ib Hizbollah’s formal withdrawal from Jurf al-Sakhar and transfer of control of the sub-district to four bodies – the Iraqi army, federal police, counter-terrorism service and Hashd – each of which is responsible for a separate geographic area. In addition, energy police have been deployed to secure oil pipelines in Jurf al-Sakhar.  Questions remain, notably over the scope of Kata’ib Hizbollah’s withdrawal. In particular, it is unclear whether Kata’ib Hizbollah will leave the central area where the 72nd and 79th Hashd brigades have been deployed – or remain there under Hashd cover. Even were Kata’ib Hizbollah to fully withdraw, it is also unclear how the prime minister will view a continued role for the Hashd in the long term. Will he consider the replacement of Kata’ib Hizbollah by other Hashd brigades as an acceptable solution? Or will he see it as essentially redistributing influence over parts of Jurf al-Sakhr without touching the underlying problem of lack of effective government oversight?  The outcome to date is cause for satisfaction in the Iraqi government. But a more sustainable solution, and one more consistent with the government’s agenda, would need to clarify the chain of command, establish full government control of the sub-district and facilitate the return of its displaced residents.  Related Tags More for you Commentary / Middle East & North Africa The U.S.-led Anti-ISIS Coalition is Leaving Iraq: What Happens Next? item.title: From Working Group to SIG Architecture: spotlight on AI Conformance
item.description: In this SIG Architecture spotlight we talked with Janet Kuo (Google) and Yuan Tang (TensorScale AI) about the journey of AI Conformance in Kubernetes, from the initial Working Group to the integration SIG Architecture as a subproject. Introductions Frederico Muñoz and Kirti Goyal (FK): Hi Janet, Yuan, and thank you for the opportunity to learn a bit more about AI Conformance. Can you tell us a bit about yourselves and how you got involved in Kubernetes? Janet Kuo : I'm a Senior Staff Software Engineer at Google and have been a Kubernetes maintainer since 2015, joining the community just as we were racing toward the 1.0 launch. I started my journey writing the core workload controllers that standardized how applications are orchestrated on Kubernetes. Today, I lead SIG Apps as a Co-chair & TL, and also lead the AI Conformance program . My current focus is to ensure Kubernetes remains the best platform for the next generation of workloads, such as AI. Yuan Tang : I'm a co-founder of TensorScale AI where we build AI infrastructure for world models. Prior to that, I was a Senior Principal Software Engineer at Red Hat, where I led the development of Red Hat AI platform and upstream open source strategy. I became involved in Kubernetes early on by fostering collaborations between the Kubernetes community and projects I was leading, including Kubeflow, Argo, and KServe. I later helped found and lead WG Serving and the AI Conformance program, advancing innovation and strengthening community collaboration around running AI workloads on Kubernetes. Program, Working Group, Subproject: the many shapes of AI Conformance FK: AI Conformance started as a CNCF Program, was it then you got involved? Janet Kuo: I was actually involved from day one since I pitched the original idea. It became obvious then that everyone was starting to run AI on Kubernetes, but vendors were building their infrastructure stacks in different ways. I got worried about ecosystem fragmentation. So I wrote up the initial Kubernetes AI Conformance Proposal, took it to the CNCF leadership to get their buy-in, and started the AI Conformance Program. Once we had the green light, I reached out to my fellow co-chairs Yuan Tang, Rita Zhang, and Mario Fahlandt to get the community rallied around it. Yuan Tang: Yes. I was a co-chair of WG Serving at that time and some of the initiatives such as the Gateway AI Inference Extension quickly gained traction. There was a strong interest among the community to include inference-related requirements in the Kubernetes AI Conformance program. FK: How would you describe the motivation behind the creation of the AI Conformance Working Group? Janet and Yuan : The motivation behind creating the Kubernetes AI Conformance Working Group (AI WG) was to address the rapid convergence of AI workloads onto Kubernetes while preventing ecosystem fragmentation. As AI adoption accelerated, organizations began running increasingly complex workloads, including distributed training, large-scale inference, GPU-intensive pipelines, and emerging agentic AI systems across many different Kubernetes platforms. However, vendors were implementing AI infrastructure capabilities differently, especially around GPUs, networking, scheduling, and inference orchestration. That created portability challenges, operational inconsistency, and growing vendor lock-in concerns. The AI WG was formed to bring the community together around: vendor-neutral AI infrastructure standards, interoperable Kubernetes-based AI platforms, consistent operational behavior for AI workloads, and common requirements for scalable AI deployment. FK: WGs are temporary by nature, based on outcomes: would you say the main goals of the WG were achieved? Janet and Yuan : Yes, the WG achieved its primary initial goals. The WG has succeeded in moving the ecosystem from: fragmented, vendor-specific AI infrastructure approaches to a shared, community-defined baseline for AI workloads on Kubernetes. Some concrete indicators of success include: Launching the Certified Kubernetes AI Conformance Program Defining formal Kubernetes AI Requirements (KARs) Getting broad participation from major ecosystem players Growing certified platforms from 18 to 31 within a few months Aligning around newer Kubernetes primitives needed for AI workloads Establishing a roadmap for automated conformance verification Most importantly, the WG created consensus that AI workloads are now a first-class Kubernetes use case. FK: AI Conformance was specifically highlighted at the latest KubeCon: is this a reflection of the growing importance of AI throughout the project? Janet and Yuan : Yes, the prominence of AI Conformance at the latest KubeCon + CloudNativeCon is a strong reflection of how central AI has become to the Kubernetes ecosystem overall. A few years ago, AI workloads on Kubernetes were still viewed as somewhat specialized, mostly tied to ML platforms or GPU-heavy research environments. What’s changed is that AI is now becoming a mainstream infrastructure concern for nearly every large-scale platform operator. That shift naturally elevates AI from an application running on Kubernetes to a core workload category Kubernetes must optimize for. The AI Conformance initiative reflects that evolution. It signals that the community now sees AI infrastructure requirements, things like accelerator scheduling, high-performance networking, workload-aware orchestration, and low-latency inference, as important enough to standardize at the ecosystem level. Its visibility at KubeCon also shows a broader strategic realization: if Kubernetes is going to remain the universal control plane for modern infrastructure, it needs to provide a consistent foundation for AI workloads across clouds, on-prem, and edge environments. So the emphasis on AI Conformance is not just about chasing AI hype; it's about Kubernetes adapting to a major shift in workload patterns and ensuring the ecosystem evolves cohesively rather than fragmenting into vendor-specific AI stacks. From Working Group to SIG Architecture subproject FK: How would you describe the change from WG to SIG? Is it a reflection of AI as something that requires ongoing architectural governance? Janet and Yuan : In Kubernetes, Working Groups are meant to be temporary. Our WG had a specific goal to get the initial Kubernetes AI Conformance requirements published and get the certification process off the ground. Once we hit those milestones, we archived the WG and moved AI Conformance to be a permanent subproject under SIG Architecture. Moving to SIG Architecture definitely proves that AI needs ongoing governance. AI isn’t just a passing trend or a one-off workload. It has become a core part of what Kubernetes runs every day. Because SIG Architecture already owns overall Kubernetes Conformance and API design principles, housing the AI Conformance subproject there makes perfect sense. It makes sure our AI Conformance requirements stay aligned with the rest of the Kubernetes ecosystem for the long haul. FK: And with that change, how would you describe the main goals and areas of intervention of the subproject? Janet and Yuan : Now that we’re a subproject, our main goal is to keep the AI Conformance standards current, vendor-neutral, and standard-setting. We want to make sure Kubernetes captures the latest advancements in AI infrastructure while keeping the ecosystem fair for everyone. When we find gaps where no clear community pattern exists, we help foster and form new standards to solve them. AI Conformance and Kubernetes FK: AI Infrastructure is evolving very quickly, while Kubernetes APIs are designed to remain stable for years. Is this something you consider a challenge? Janet and Yuan : It’s definitely a tricky balance. AI moves very fast, while Kubernetes is designed to be stable and boring. But we actually structured the program around this exact tension. First, we use a tiered graduation model. When new AI infrastructure concepts emerge, we introduce them as recommended SHOULD requirements. That gives the ecosystem room to experiment and agree on best practices without locking Kubernetes into rigid APIs too early. Once those APIs stabilize and with ecosystem adoption, we graduate them to mandatory MUST requirements. Second, we intentionally keep our focus on the infrastructure layer. We test for core capabilities like accelerator support through Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA), rather than getting bogged down in specific AI frameworks or model servers. That keeps the base platform stable while letting the AI tooling evolve as fast as it needs to. FK: DRA has evolved, also due to the work of WG Device Management, as an important part of Kubernetes (and especially so for AI workloads), with SIG Architecture having an important role in how it’s integrated in Kubernetes: do you find any parallel in this? Specifically, do you think there will be a heavier focus in the integration with the evolving Kubernetes architecture as part of SIG Architecture? Janet and Yuan : There is a huge parallel there. Whenever we face a massive, complicated challenge that touches multiple parts of the codebase and involves multiple SIGs, a Working Group is the best place to start. It lets experts from different SIGs get together to figure out the problem, and build consensus. Being part of SIG Architecture means there will be a much heavier focus on how AI capabilities weave into the evolving Kubernetes architecture. Instead of treating AI as an add-on layer, we’re looking at how core Kubernetes primitives, like scheduling and resource allocation, need to adapt at a foundational level to support the next decade of AI workloads. Final remarks FK: For interested contributors, what’s the best way to get involved with the AI Conformance subproject? Janet and Yuan : We're always looking for new contributors. The easiest way to get started is by checking out our main repo at kubernetes-sigs/ai-conformance and join our meetings . If you're interested in defining new AI Conformance requirements, you can jump into PR reviews or propose your own using our KAR template . If you want to write code, we always need help expanding our automated Go test suites in the test/ directory . For vendors looking to certify their platforms, all the details are at cncf/k8s-ai-conformance . FK: Any final comments you would like to share? Janet and Yuan : We’ve been blown away by how fast the community has rallied around this. When we first announced the AI Conformance program during the keynote at KubeCon NA 2025 , we weren’t sure what the response would be. But by the time we gave our update keynote at KubeCon EU 2026 , we had grown from 18 certified platforms to 31 in just a few months. That kind of growth shows just how much the industry wanted a unified, vendor-neutral standard. It gives organizations the confidence that they can run their AI workloads on any certification Kubernetes platform without getting locked into a proprietary stack. item.title: Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement
item.description: The concept of recursive self-improvement (RSI) dates back to I. J. Good (1965) , where he defined an “ultraintelligent machine” as a system that can surpass humans in all intellectual activities and design better machines to improve itself. Yudkowsky (2008) used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” for a specific feedback loop: an AI uses its current intelligence to improve the cognitive machinery that produces its intelligence. This feedback loop in modern AI may indicate the model rewriting its own weights directly, or more broadly the model improves the training pipeline and the deployment system , which in turn enables a better successor model with improved performance across economically valuable tasks. The speed of research development in AI has been shown to drastically accelerated in frontier labs ( Anthropic ; OpenAI ).

item.title: Common pitfalls when building generative AI applications
item.description: As we’re still in the early days of building applications with foundation models, it’s normal to make mistakes. This is a quick note with examples of some of the most common pitfalls that I’ve seen, both from public case studies and from my personal experience. Because these pitfalls are common, if you’ve worked on any AI product, you’ve probably seen them before. 1. Use generative AI when you don't need generative AI Every time there’s a new technology, I can hear the collective sigh of senior engineers everywhere: “Not everything is a nail.” Generative AI isn’t an exception — its seemingly limitless capabilities only exacerbate the tendency to use generative AI for everything. A team pitched me the idea of using generative AI to optimize energy consumption. They fed a household’s list of energy-intensive activities and hourly electricity prices into an LLM, then asked it to create a schedule to minimize energy costs. Their experiments showed that this could help reduce a household’s electricity bill by 30%. Free money. Why wouldn’t anyone want to use their app? I asked: “How does it compare to simply scheduling the most energy-intensive activities when electricity is cheapest? Say, doing your laundry and charging your car after 10pm?” They said they would try it later and let me know. They never followed up, but they abandoned this app soon after. I suspect that this greedy scheduling can be quite effective. Even if it’s not, there are other much cheaper and more reliable optimization solutions than generative AI, like linear programming. I’ve seen this scenario over and over again. A big company wants to use generative AI to detect anomalies in network traffic. Another wants to predict upcoming customer call volume. A hospital wants to detect whether a patient is malnourished (really not recommended). It can often be beneficial to explore a new approach to get a sense of what’s possible, as long as you’re aware that your goal isn’t to solve a problem but to test a solution. “We solve the problem” and “We use generative AI” are two very different headlines, and unfortunately, so many people would rather have the latter. 2. Confuse 'bad product' with 'bad AI' At the other end of the spectrum, many teams dismiss gen AI as a valid solution for their problems because they tried it out and their users hated it. However, other teams successfully used gen AI for similar use cases. I could only look into two of these teams. In both cases, the issue wasn’t with AI, but with product. Many people have told me that the technical aspects of their AI applications are straightforward. The hard part is user experience (UX). What should the product interface look like? How to seamlessly integrate the product into the user workflow? How to incorporate human-in-the-loop? UX has always been challenging, but it’s even more so with generative AI. While we know that generative AI is changing how we read, write, learn, teach, work, entertain, etc., we don’t quite know how yet. What will the future of reading/learning/working be like? Here are some simple examples to show how what users want can be counter-intuitive and need rigorous user study. My friend works on an application that summarizes meeting transcripts. Initially, her team focused on getting the right summary length. Would users prefer 3-sentence summaries or 5-sentence summaries? However, it turned out that their users didn’t care about the actual summary. They only wanted action items specific to them from each meeting. When LinkedIn developed a chatbot for skill fit assessment, they discovered that users didn’t want correct responses. Users wanted helpful responses. For example, if a user asks a bot whether they’re a fit for a job and the bot responds with: “You’re a terrible fit,” this response might be correct but not very helpful to the user. Users want tips on what the gaps are and what they can do to close the gaps. Intuit built a chatbot to help users answer tax questions. Initially, they got lukewarm feedback — users didn’t find the bot useful. After investigation, they found out that users actually hated typing. Facing a blank chatbot, users didn’t know what the bot could do and what to type. So, for each interaction, Intuit added a few suggested questions for users to click on. This reduced the friction for users to use the bot and gradually built users’ trust. The feedback from users then became much more positive. (Shared by Nhung Ho , VP of AI at Intuit, during our panel at Grace Hopper.) Because everyone uses the same models nowadays, the AI components of AI products are similar, and the differentiation is product. 3. Start too complex Examples of this pitfall: Use an agentic framework when direct API calls work. Agonize over what vector database to use when a simple term-based retrieval solution (that doesn’t require a vectordb) works. Insist on finetuning when prompting works. Use semantic caching. Given so many shiny new technologies, it’s tempting to jump straight into using them. However, incorporating external tools too early can cause 2 problems: Abstract away critical details, making it hard to understand and debug your system. Introduce unnecessary bugs. Tool developers can make mistakes. For example, I often find typos in default prompts when reviewing a framework’s codebase. If the framework you use updates its prompt without telling you, your application’s behaviors might change and you might not know why. Eventually, abstractions are good. But abstractions need to incorporate best practices and be tested overtime. As we’re still in the early days of AI engineering, best practices are still evolving, we should be more vigilant when adopting any abstraction. 4. Over-index on early success It took LinkedIn 1 month to achieve 80% of the experience they wanted, and an additional 4 months to surpass 95% . The initial success made them grossly underestimate how challenging it is to improve the product, especially around hallucinations. They found it discouraging how difficult it was to achieve each subsequent 1% gain. A startup that develops AI sales assistants for ecommerce told me that getting from 0 to 80% took as long as from 80% to 90% . The challenges they faced: Accuracy/latency tradeoff: more planning/self-correction = more nodes = higher latency Tool calling: hard for agents to differentiate similar tools Hard for tonal requests (e.g. "talk like a luxury brand concierge" ) in the system prompt to be perfectly obeyed Hard for the agent to completely understand customers’ intent Hard to create a specific set of unit tests because the combination of queries is basically infinite Thanks Jason Tjahjono for sharing this. In the paper UltraChat, Ding et al. (2023) shared that “ the journey from 0 to 60 is easy, whereas progressing from 60 to 100 becomes exceedingly challenging .” This is perhaps one of the first painful lessons anyone who has built an AI product quickly learns. It’s easy to build a demo, but hard to build a product. Other than the issues of hallucinations, latency, latency/accuracy tradeoff, tool use, prompting, testing, … as mentioned, teams also run into issues, such as: Reliability from the API providers. A team told me that 10% of their API calls timed out. Or product’s behaviors change because the underlying model changes. Compliance , e.g. around AI output copyrights, data access/sharing, user privacy, security risks from retrieval/caching systems, and ambiguity around training data lineage. Safety , e.g. bad actors abusing your product, your product generates insensitive or offensive responses. When planning a product’s milestones and resources, make sure to take into account these potential roadblocks. A friend calls this “being cautiously optimistic”. However, remember that many cool demos don’t lead to wonderful products. 5. Forgo human evaluation To automatically evaluate AI applications, many teams opt for the AI-as-a-judge (also called LLM-as-a-judge) approach — using AI models to evaluate AI outputs. A common pitfall is forgoing human evaluation to rely entirely on AI judges. While AI judges can be very useful, they aren’t deterministic. The quality of a judge depends on the underlying judge’s model, the judge’s prompt, and the use case. If the AI judge isn’t developed properly, it can give misleading evaluations about your application’s performance. AI judges must be evaluated and iterated over time, just like all other AI applications. The teams with the best products I’ve seen all have human evaluation to supplement their automated evaluation. Every day, they have human experts evaluate a subset of their application’s outputs, which can be anywhere from 30 - 1000 examples. Daily manual evaluation serves 3 purposes: Correlate human judgments with AI judgments. If the score by human evaluators is decreasing but the score by AI judges is increasing, you might want to investigate your AI judges. Gain a better understanding of how users use your application, which can give you ideas to improve your application. Detect patterns and changes in users’ behaviors, using your knowledge of current events, that automated data exploration might miss. The reliability of human evaluation also depends on well-crafted annotation guidelines. These annotation guidelines can help improve the model’s instructions (if a human has a hard time following the instructions, the model will, too). It can also be reused to create finetuning data later if you choose to finetune. In every project I’ve worked on, staring at data for just 15 minutes usually gives me some insight that could save me hours of headaches . Greg Brockman tweeted: “ Manual inspection of data has probably the highest value-to-prestige ratio of any activity in machine learning. ” 6. Crowdsource use cases This is a mistake I saw in the early days when enterprises were in a frenzy to adopt generative AI. Unable to come up with a strategy for what use cases to focus on, many tech executives crowdsourced ideas from the whole company. “We hire smart people. Let them tell us what to do.” They then try to implement these ideas one by one. And that’s how we ended up with a million text-to-SQL models, a million Slack bots, and a billion code plugins. While it’s indeed a good idea to listen to the smart people that you hire, individuals might be biased toward the problems that immediately affect their day-to-day work instead of problems that might bring the highest returns on investment. Without an overall strategy that considers the big picture, it’s easy to get sidetracked into a series of small, low-impact applications and come to the wrong conclusion that gen AI has no ROI. Summary In short, here are the common AI engineering pitfalls: Use generative AI when you don’t need generative AI Gen AI isn’t a one-size-fits-all solution to all problems. Many problems don’t even need AI. Confuse ‘bad product’ with ‘bad AI’ For many AI product, AI is the easy part, product is the hard part. Start too complex While fancy new frameworks and finetuning can be useful for many projects, they shouldn’t be your first course of action. Over-index on early success Initial success can be misleading. Going from demo-ready to production-ready can take much longer than getting to the first demo. Forgo human evaluation AI judges should be validated and correlated with systematic human evaluation. Crowdsource use cases Have a big-picture strategy to maximize return on investment.
